title: Orcas Are Exploding Sunfish Like Piñatas, New Footage Shows
summary: Orcas have a reputation for brutal hunting tactics. They slap stingrays, punt seals into the air, and team up to knock penguins off ice floes. But scientists just documented something new: orcas smashing dead sunfish so hard the fish explode. The behavior was filmed in the Gulf of California in 2024 and 2025. In both cases, one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady while a second slammed into it with enough force to pulverize it. Researchers published the findings July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology. "I was absolutely gobsmacked," says Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand who wasn't involved in the work. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen." She isn't surprised orcas found a creative way to handle sharp-tail sunfish — those fish can grow up to a few meters (10 feet) long. "Orcas will do all sorts of things," Nyegaard says. "They are so clever at figuring out how to hunt and deal with a ton of different prey types." Why do it? Francesca Pancaldi, a marine biologist at Mexico's National Polytechnic Institute, says orcas most likely smash sunfish to break them into smaller bites for young orcas. After one explosion, a young orca fed on the pieces. But feeding may not be the only reason. "Killer whales are highly social animals," Pancaldi says. A single activity can provide nutrition, help orcas bond, and teach young whales how to hunt. So the next time you see an orca, remember: it might be a hunter, a teacher, and a piñata champion all at once.
why_it_matters: This is a snapshot of animal culture in action: a complex, apparently new hunting technique shared between adults and passed to a young orca, which shows how much of the behaviour of the ocean's top predator is still undocumented — and why that matters for understanding and protecting marine food webs.

background_read: The Gulf of California, sometimes called the Sea of Cortez, is a narrow stretch of sea between Mexico's Baja California peninsula and the mainland. It is unusually rich in marine life and is a regular feeding and breeding area for many large ocean animals, including several kinds of whales and dolphins.

Orcas, or killer whales, are actually the largest members of the dolphin family and live in every ocean. Different populations specialise in different prey — some eat fish, others hunt seals, dolphins or even large whales — and their techniques, such as punting seals into the air or working together to wash seals off ice floes, are learned from older animals rather than instinct. That makes orca hunting a form of culture passed down through generations.

Marianne Nyegaard, quoted in the article, is a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand and is known for identifying the hoodwinker sunfish, a species that had been overlooked by scientists for centuries. Frontiers in Ethology is a scientific journal; ethology is simply the study of animal behaviour.

Ocean sunfish are among the heaviest bony fish in the sea, and the sharp-tail sunfish mentioned here has a pointed tail rather than the rounded one seen in other species. Because these fish are slow and large, orcas do not need to kill them quickly — but a body that big is awkward to swallow, which helps explain why the animals might break it apart instead.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — another sign of orca intelligence and culture
perspectives.description: Supporters see this as fresh evidence that orcas are flexible problem-solvers whose techniques spread socially. The presence of a young orca feeding on the pieces suggests teaching and food-sharing, behaviours that are rare outside a few clever mammals and birds.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — two clips are not a lot of evidence
perspectives.description: Only two events, in 2024 and 2025, were analysed, and the researchers worked from footage rather than planned observations. Critics would want repeated sightings, more individuals and information about how often it happens before calling sunfish-smashing a regular orca behaviour rather than an occasional stunt.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a known pattern of culturally transmitted hunting
perspectives.description: Orca populations worldwide develop specialised foraging techniques that differ from group to group, from wave-washing seals in Antarctica to intentional beach strandings to catch sea lion pups. New techniques appearing in a population fit this well-documented pattern, and slow-moving sunfish are easy prey that does not need to be chased down first.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — from viral clips to real data
perspectives.description: The next step would be systematic surveys and underwater video to see how often sunfish are smashed, which orcas do it, and whether the skill spreads. That could also raise questions about how much orca behaviour we are still missing simply because so much of it happens out of sight.
